Seminar Title:

Smart Project Management for Mitigating Construction Delays: The Role of Integrated Planning, Project Risk Management and the Internet of Things in the Indian Construction Industry

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

School of Management

Speaker Name:

Rakesh Acharya ( Rollno : 920sm5003)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

Conference Room (SM)

Date and Time:

14 Oct 2026 16:30 hrs

Contact:

Mayank Yadav

Abstract:

Over the past decade, construction activity in India has grown to an unprecedented scale, with capital commitments to match, yet the sector's most visible shortcoming continues to be its inability to finish projects on time. When schedules slip, costs rise, contractual disputes arise, productivity and quality fall, and relationships among stakeholders deteriorate in the most serious cases a project may be suspended, taken to litigation or terminated altogether. Planning, the allocation of resources and the mitigation of risk have each been acknowledged as determinants of project performance, but the existing literature tends to treat them separately rather than as parts of a single integrated framework. Empirical evidence remains scarce on several questions: whether and how the separate delay causes behave as an interacting system how these three planning dimensions jointly shape delay in construction what contribution digital technologies, among them the Internet of Things (IoT), make to reinforcing the link that connects risk management with project performance and what it actually means, in managerial rather than technological terms, for construction projects to be run in a smart manner.

An extensive survey of the literature, supplemented by consultation with practitioners from industry and with academic experts, was used to identify the decision-making variables, and the research proceeds through three interlinked studies. In the first, delay is treated as a system of interdependent causes: sixteen factors, drawn from a reading of the literature organised around legal, environmental, technological, social, economic and political (PESTEL) dimensions and endorsed by eight experts of senior standing, are arranged hierarchically using total interpretive structural modeling (TISM) and then sorted according to their driving power and dependence power by means of fuzzy MICMAC (cross-impact matrix multiplication applied to classification) analysis. A second study builds a conceptual framework that rests on uncertainty management theory, on organisational behaviour theory and on the digital transformation literature its latent constructs are resource management and governance, internal organisational culture, project stakeholder communication, quality improvement and financial efficiency, together with project risk management, smart project management and the IoT, and the framework is tested by structural equation modeling on responses from 360 construction industry stakeholders across the four regions of India. The last of the three studies goes beyond the mitigation of delay and asks what it is that makes the management of a construction project smart. Taking general systems theory as its basis, it defines smart project management in terms of five managerial characteristics (being specific, measurable, assignable, realistic and time-bound), connects five foundational project management domains to project risk management and links project risk management, in its turn, to smart project management the resulting framework is tested on a survey of 399 construction professionals using confirmatory factor analysis together with covariance-based structural equation modeling.

Study one identified scope creep, ambiguous contractual procedures, inadequate planning, poor communication, and disputes and negotiations as the delay drivers of greatest weight, and showed that interference by the developer, late payment, changes to specifications and late procurement act as channels through which instability spreads across the system it also showed that IoT-enabled monitoring yields its benefits only where sound governance, clear contracts and competent planning are already in place. Study two indicates that schedule overruns fall markedly where planning is of high quality, resources are better aligned and risk mitigation practices are developed proactively. In that study project risk management proved to be the central mediator: it is the channel by which financial efficiency, stakeholder communication, organisational culture, resource management and planning quality are converted into project performance, and the IoT significantly reinforces this relationship, which indicates that digital technology amplifies sound managerial practice rather than substituting for it. Study three established that every one of the five managerial domains has a positive association with the project risk management construct, planning and scheduling carrying the largest standardised coefficient, and that project risk management is in turn strongly and positively related to smart project management this places it as the cross-functional capability that connects foundational project management practice with structured managerial action.

Taken together, the three studies show that technology cannot deliver its benefits until the structural sources of delay located in communication, planning, contracting and governance have been dealt with that managing construction projects smartly depends on integrating the quality of planning with the allocation of resources and the mitigation of risk and that smartness of a managerial kind, which finds expression in the disciplined management of risk, is both different from technological smartness and a prerequisite for it. From these findings the research derives implications for theory, for management and for policy, addressed to policymakers and practitioners, with the aim of supporting integrated planning frameworks that make schedules more predictable, lower cost overruns and raise the overall performance of Indian construction projects.
